source_refs.note: 2. Non-Point Source (NPS) Pollution: a main subheading of 33.2 Sources of Water Pollution, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 249-250.

blocks.text: Non-point source pollution, also known as diffused pollution, occurs when rainfall or snowmelt moves over and through the ground. As the water moves, it picks up and carries away natural and human-made pollutants, finally depositing them into lakes, rivers, wetlands, and coastal waters. Unlike point sources, NPS pollution is heavily dependent on weather events like heavy storms. It results in a mixture of various pollutants at lower concentrations across a much wider area. Some examples of non-point pollution sources are:

items: Rain washing excess ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃), fertilizers, and pesticides from thousands of hectares of farmland into a river system.
Stormwater moving over impermeable surfaces (roads and car parks), collecting leaked engine oils (hydrocarbons), zinc from tires, and road salts.

blocks.prompt:
a) Classify these as point or non-point sources of water pollution, explain your choice.
(i) The outfall pipes used to release treated sewage into a bay or river from wastewater treatment plants.
(ii) The “acid rain” caused by the nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) from distant traffic or power stations dissolved in rainwater.
blocks.explanation:
(i) Point source: the water comes from a single, identifiable pipe.
(ii) Non-point source: the NOₓ comes from many distant sources and falls with rain over a wide area; it depends on the weather.

blocks.prompt: b) Give two major differences between point and non-point pollution sources.
blocks.explanation: A point source comes from a single identifiable location, and the concentration near it is very high. A non-point source comes from a wide area, spreads far at low concentration, and depends on weather such as rain or storms.

rows: From one identifiable location (a pipe, a leaking tank)
From many places over a wide area (fields, roads)
Very high concentration at the point of discharge (plume, acute toxicity)
Many pollutants spread far at low concentration
Does not depend much on the weather
Depends strongly on weather such as rain, snowmelt and storms
